concepts.name: Service names, the default network and ports

questions.prompt: In a Compose file, the Postgres service is called `db` and has `ports: ["15432:5432"]`. Which host and port should the `api` service use in its `DATABASE_URL`?

choices.text: `localhost:15432`
The `db` container's IP address, from `docker inspect`

questions.explanation: Compose puts every service on a default network where each one is reachable by its service name, and service-to-service traffic uses the container port, 5432. The host port 15432 is only for reaching Postgres from outside that network, such as `psql` on your laptop. Container IPs change when containers are recreated, so always use the name.

sources.title: Networking in Compose
sources.claim: Compose creates a default network on which services find each other by service name, service-to-service traffic uses the container port while the host port is for outside access, and container IPs change so services should be referenced by name.

questions.prompt: What does `ports: ["15432:5432"]` on the `db` service do?

choices.text: It makes other containers reach Postgres at `db:15432` instead of 5432
It tells Postgres to listen on port 15432 inside the container instead of on 5432
It is required before any other service on the network can reach `db`
It maps host port 15432 to the container's 5432; other containers still use 5432

questions.explanation: The format is `HOST:CONTAINER`. Publishing a port only opens a path from the host into the container. Containers on the same Compose network can already reach `db` on 5432 without any `ports` entry. Leave `ports` off services the host doesn't need to reach, which keeps them off the host's network.

sources.title: Define services in Docker Compose
sources.claim: The ports short syntax is [HOST:]CONTAINER[/PROTOCOL], mapping a host port to a container port.

questions.prompt: Postgres keeps its data in a named volume `pgdata` declared in the Compose file's top-level `volumes`. Which command deletes that data?

choices.text: `docker compose down -v`
`docker compose down`
`docker compose restart db`
`docker compose stop`

questions.explanation: `docker compose down` removes the containers and networks but keeps named volumes, so the next `up` finds your data again. The `-v` (`--volumes`) flag also removes the named volumes declared in the file and anonymous volumes. `stop` and `restart` don't remove anything.

sources.title: docker compose down
sources.claim: By default down removes the service containers and networks, and only with -v/--volumes does it also remove named volumes declared in the file and anonymous volumes.

sources.title: Volumes
sources.claim: A volume's contents exist outside any container's lifecycle, whereas a container's writable layer is destroyed together with the container.

questions.prompt: Your `db` service has no volume at all. You create some tables, run `docker compose down`, then `docker compose up`. What happened to the tables?

choices.text: They are still there, because Compose keeps each service's data
They are there, but read-only
They are gone: they lived in the removed container's writable layer
They are saved into the `postgres` image for next time

questions.explanation: Without a volume, Postgres writes into the container's writable layer, and `down` removes the container along with that layer. A new container starts from the unchanged image. A volume's contents exist outside any container's lifecycle, which is why databases in Compose get a named volume.

questions.prompt: Your project folder has a `.env` file with `LOG_LEVEL=debug`, and `compose.yaml` has `image: "myapp:${TAG}"` but no `environment` or `env_file` entries. What does `.env` do here?

choices.text: It sets `LOG_LEVEL` inside every container the project starts
Nothing, unless you pass `--env-file .env` to `docker compose up` yourself
It is copied into the image at build time and read by the app
It fills `${...}` in the Compose file; its values don't reach the containers

questions.explanation: Compose loads `.env` from the project directory by default and uses it for interpolation, such as `${TAG}`. The Docker docs stress that interpolating a value doesn't put it in a container's environment. To pass a variable in, list it under `environment` (for example `LOG_LEVEL: ${LOG_LEVEL}`) or name a file under `env_file`.

sources.title: Set, use, and manage variables in a Compose file with interpolation
sources.claim: When --env-file is not given, Compose uses variables from the .env file in the project directory to interpolate ${...} expressions in the Compose file.

sources.title: Set environment variables within your container's environment
sources.claim: A container's environment is not set until the service configuration has an explicit entry, such as environment or env_file, that sets it.

questions.prompt: The `api` service has `env_file: [api.env]`, where `api.env` sets `LOG_LEVEL=info`, and also `environment: {LOG_LEVEL: debug}`. What does the container see?

choices.text: `LOG_LEVEL=info`, because `env_file` is read last
`LOG_LEVEL=debug`, because `environment` overrides `env_file`
Both values, joined by a comma
Compose refuses to start because the variable is set twice

questions.explanation: The Compose file reference says variables declared in the `environment` section override values from `env_file`. That makes `env_file` a good place for shared defaults and `environment` the place for per-service overrides.

sources.title: Define services in Docker Compose
sources.claim: The services reference says variables declared in the environment section override values loaded from env_file.

questions.prompt: You give the `api` service a Compose secret `db_password`, defined with `file: ./db_password.txt`. How does the app read it?

choices.text: From the read-only file `/run/secrets/db_password`
From the environment variable `DB_PASSWORD`
From `./db_password.txt` in the container's working directory
From a `SECRET_DB_PASSWORD` build argument

questions.explanation: Compose mounts each secret a service is granted as a read-only file at `/run/secrets/<secret_name>`. It doesn't become an environment variable, which is the point: environment variables are visible to every process and easy to leak into logs. Some official images, such as `postgres`, read secrets through `_FILE` variables like `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE`.

sources.title: Manage secrets securely in Docker Compose
sources.claim: Compose mounts secrets as files at /run/secrets/<secret_name> and recommends them over environment variables, which are visible to all processes and can leak into logs; images like postgres support _FILE variables.

sources.title: Define services in Docker Compose
sources.claim: A granted secret is mounted read-only at /run/secrets/<secret_name> inside the container, with mode 0444 by default.

questions.prompt: The `api` service has `depends_on: [db]` (short syntax). On `docker compose up`, the API sometimes crashes with 'connection refused'. Why?

choices.text: Short syntax only records a link between services and doesn't affect start order
With the short syntax, Compose starts `db` after `api`, not before it
Compose starts `db` first but doesn't wait for Postgres to accept connections
`depends_on` only works for services built from a Dockerfile, not images

questions.explanation: Short syntax guarantees `db` is started before `api`, but Compose waits only until the container is running, not until it is ready. Postgres needs a few seconds to accept connections. Add a `healthcheck` to `db` (such as `pg_isready`) and use the long syntax `depends_on: {db: {condition: service_healthy}}`.

sources.title: Control startup and shutdown order in Compose
sources.claim: Compose waits only until a dependency container is running, not ready; the example uses a pg_isready healthcheck with $$-escaped variables and depends_on condition service_healthy.

sources.title: Define services in Docker Compose
sources.claim: Short-syntax depends_on only guarantees dependencies are started first, while condition service_healthy makes Compose wait for the dependency's healthcheck to pass.

questions.prompt: Docker's startup-order example uses `test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"]`. Why `$$` instead of `$`?

choices.text: `$$` marks the variable as required, so Compose fails if it's unset
It escapes `$` from Compose, so the shell in the container expands the variable
`CMD-SHELL` needs every special character doubled to reach the shell
It tells Compose to read the value from the host's `.env` file instead of the shell

questions.explanation: Compose interpolates `${VAR}` itself, from your shell and `.env`, before the container starts. `$$` is a literal dollar sign, so Compose leaves the variable alone and the check's shell, inside the `db` container, expands it from the container's own environment, where `POSTGRES_USER` is set. The required-variable syntax is `${VAR:?error}`.

sources.title: Interpolation
sources.claim: $$ produces a literal dollar sign and stops Compose interpolating the value, so the variable is left for the container to resolve; ${VAR:?error} is the required-value syntax.

questions.prompt: Describe a Compose file where one `docker compose up` brings up your API, Postgres with pgvector and Redis, and the API starts only once the others are healthy. Name the key parts.

model_answer.summary: Three services, healthchecks on Postgres and Redis, `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` on the API, a named volume for Postgres data, and the API reaching the others by service name.
key_points: An `api` service built from the Dockerfile, a `db` service from a Postgres image that includes pgvector, and a `redis` service
`db` has a `healthcheck` such as `pg_isready`, and `redis` one such as `redis-cli ping` (which replies `PONG`)
`api` uses long-syntax `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` for both, because short syntax doesn't wait for readiness
A named volume mounted into `db` so the data survives `docker compose down`
The API connects to `db:5432` and `redis:6379`, with the database password from a secret or env file, not hard-coded

questions.explanation: 'Up healthy' means each dependency proves it is ready before its dependents start, which is what healthchecks plus `service_healthy` give you. Without them the API races the database on every cold start. `docker compose ps` shows each service's health so you can check the result.

questions.prompt: Compare `.env`, `env_file`, `environment` and Compose secrets. Which would you use for the database password, and why?

model_answer.summary: `.env` fills `${...}` in the Compose file, `env_file` and `environment` set variables inside containers (with `environment` winning), and secrets mount files; use a secret for the password because environment variables leak easily.
key_points: `.env` in the project directory is used for interpolating the Compose file, and doesn't reach containers by itself
`env_file` loads variables from a file into a service's container; `environment` sets them inline and overrides `env_file`
A secret is mounted read-only at `/run/secrets/<name>`, so it isn't in the environment
Environment variables are visible to every process in the container and can end up in logs, which is why Docker recommends secrets for sensitive values
Keep the secret's source file and any `.env` with real values out of git and out of the build context

questions.explanation: The four look alike but act at different times and places: `.env` when Compose reads the file, `env_file` and `environment` when the container starts, secrets as files at run time. Mixing up the first two is the most common reason a variable 'isn't set' inside a container.

questions.prompt: Your API works when you run it on your laptop against Postgres in Compose, using `localhost:15432`. Inside Compose, with the same URL, it can't connect. Explain why and what to change.

model_answer.summary: Inside a container, `localhost` is that container itself, not the host or the database container; on the Compose network the API must use the service name and container port, `db:5432`.
key_points: Each container has its own network interface, so `localhost` inside the API container points at the API container
Compose creates a default network for the project, and each service is reachable there by its service name through Compose's DNS
Service-to-service traffic uses the container port (5432); the host port (15432) is only for access from outside that network
So set the API's URL to `db:5432` in Compose, for example through an environment variable, and keep `localhost:15432` for tools on the laptop
Don't use container IP addresses: they change when containers are recreated

questions.explanation: Moving code into a container changes what 'this machine' means. The fix is configuration, not code: read the database host from an environment variable so the same image works on a laptop and in Compose.
